trigger: adding a new Connector subclass, or the first run of any pipeline against one
what_went_wrong: MultiCsvJoinConnector was implemented with only the read path. The first run against it died in the quality node with "connector 'returns_risk_orders' cannot materialise a local clean layer; emit warehouse DDL instead" — materialize_clean/drop_clean/materialize_scores were never written, even though the connector owns a private in-process DuckDB engine and could inherit CsvDuckDBConnector's implementations almost verbatim.
rule: A Connector subclass backed by a locally writable engine must implement the whole write-side contract — materialize_clean, drop_clean, materialize_scores — before its first run, not just test_connection/get_schema/_execute. Without them the quality node fails on first use and model output can never be measured as SQL, only derived.
promoted: atlas/connectors/multi_csv_join.py — the three methods are implemented in code (mechanical)

trigger: the quality node / run_copilot() executing against a wide table (20+ columns) or a joined view
what_went_wrong: run_copilot() called detect_issues() three times (directly, inside clean_layer.build_plan(), and again inside clean_layer.apply()'s internal build_plan()) and build_plan() twice. Invisible on a 6-10 column file; on a 36-column joined view detect_issues alone cost ~26s, so the redundancy added ~80s and pushed the quality node past its 180s timeout, failing the run.
rule: Treat detect_issues()/build_plan() as expensive and O(columns): any quality entry point must thread an already-computed issues list and CleanPlan down to build_plan()/apply() instead of letting them recompute. Node timeouts are sized for narrow single-file sources and a wide joined view is where the redundancy first bites.
promoted: atlas/quality/clean_layer.py + atlas/quality/pipeline.py — issues=/plan= passthrough in code; ~157s to ~104s on the same table, 380 tests green (mechanical). Known residual: guardrails.py::column_guardrails() still re-detects on the clean table (advisory path, smaller magnitude, deliberately left).

trigger: binding a binary target on a joined source that carries more than one outcome flag derived from the same underlying event
what_went_wrong: The returns_risk_orders view carries product_quality_return, non_quality_return, any_return, return_reason and return_status side by side. binding.py::split_features excludes only the bound target and entity, so for target=product_quality_return every sibling outcome column stayed a feature candidate and handed the model its own label under a different name.
rule: When a source carries several outcome columns derived from one event, give each target its own modeling view that explicitly EXCLUDEs every sibling outcome column (SELECT * EXCLUDE (...) in DuckDB). The generic binder has no domain knowledge of sibling outcomes and will never catch this for you.

trigger: before the FIRST fit of any interpretable model on a joined star-schema source carrying dimension attributes
what_went_wrong: The feature set kept a fine-grained identity categorical (store_name, 15 levels) alongside coarser attributes that are exact functions of it (store_city/district/region, then store_type/opening_year/size_sqm), plus dominant_category under dominant_subcategory and customer_region under customer_city. One-hot encoded, the coarser dummies are exact linear combinations of the finer ones, so the design matrix was rank-deficient (99 of 148 columns). The real error was procedural: hierarchies were fixed one at a time as each fit failed, so the same mistake burned three separate runs.
rule: Sweep EVERY feature pair for exact functional determinism in one pass before the first fit — for each candidate pair, SELECT finer, count(DISTINCT coarser) FROM t GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(DISTINCT coarser) > 1 must return zero rows — and drop the coarser column of every hierarchy in a single edit. Never discover a schema's hierarchies one failed fit at a time.

trigger: assembling a feature set that contains ID-like numerics, derived flags, or two numerics that might coincide on this particular dataset
what_went_wrong: store_id was a 1:1 relabelling of store_name and meaningless as a continuous feature; is_single_line_order is by construction CASE WHEN num_line_items = 1; and num_distinct_products happened to equal num_line_items on all 12,000 rows because no order in this dataset repeats a product across lines — an accidental duplicate that no amount of schema reading would reveal.
rule: Exclude arbitrary ID numerics from continuous features, exclude any flag that is a CASE over another included column, and test numeric-vs-numeric EXACT equality on the actual data, not on the schema — a duplicate that exists only in this extract still makes the design singular.

trigger: two categoricals where one nests inside the other only partially (brand within subcategory), after the pairwise determinism sweep came back clean
what_went_wrong: dominant_brand does not determine dominant_subcategory in aggregate (Samsung spans 5 subcategories) so the pairwise check gave an all-clear, yet the design was still short 3 dimensions: some brands (Asus, Canon) sit in exactly one subcategory, and their dummies are exact linear combinations of that subcategory's block. It was found only by computing numpy.linalg.matrix_rank on the encoded matrix and removing columns greedily.
rule: A pairwise "does A determine B" check is necessary but never sufficient. Before trusting a fit, encode the design the way the engine does (logit.build_design, drop_first=True) and assert numpy.linalg.matrix_rank(X) == X.shape[1]; when short, greedily drop whole source-column blocks to name the offender rather than guessing.

trigger: a lifecycle/status column that records whether the event creating the target's linked record occurred at all
what_went_wrong: After every rank problem was fixed the fit still failed with "logistic fit did not converge". order_status was the cause: both return targets are deterministically 0 for all 10,442 Completed and 495 Cancelled orders, because a return record can only exist for a returned order. The model could near-perfectly predict the majority class, so the MLE diverged — quasi-complete separation, not rank deficiency.
rule: A status column describing whether the target's linked record could exist at all is leakage-adjacent even when the target is a subtype of that event; exclude it. Recognise both symptoms of the same mistake: rank deficiency AND "did not converge". Confirm with SQL that the target is deterministically constant outside one status value before blaming the optimiser.
